part1-can-two-walk-together-except-they-.reason: Opens on the order of Amos 3:3's clauses, but the why (unasked questions get filled with private assumptions, and the disagreement only grows in price) arrives mid-lesson; the unspoken question is never named up front.
part1-can-two-walk-together-except-they-.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why does agreement have to come before the walk? Because in Amos 3:3 agreement is the condition that makes walking together possible at all. The hard questions partners leave unasked do not go away. Each one fills the blank with his own assumption, and the disagreement waits until it is expensive. Here is what the Word shows, and the four questions to settle first.
part1-can-two-walk-together-except-they-.example: TWO PLANS, ONE FIRST YEAR. Say two partners buy a rental together. One is quietly building retirement income for twenty years. The other plans to sell in four. Their first year looks identical: same building, same tenants, same work. Nobody asked about purpose, because things were going well. In year four one wants to sell and the other refuses. Neither partner changed. The disagreement was there on day one, and it simply grew in price.
part1-can-two-walk-together-except-they-.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why does agreement come before the walk? Because the disagreement that surfaces in year three was already there on day one, and time only raises its price. So settle purpose, authority, money and exit before you start. If that conversation ends the partnership, it has succeeded early, at almost no cost. Yahweh's question in Amos is not a warning against walking together. It is an instruction about what has to happen first.

teen.open: Why agree before you start something together? Because the questions you skip do not disappear. They come back later, bigger and harder.
teen.close: So why does agreement come first? Because talking it through early is cheap, and finding out late costs a lot. Agree, then walk.

senior.open: Amos 3:3 places agreement before walking together, and the order matters. Questions left unasked at the start are quietly answered by each party's own assumptions.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. Agreement must come first because the disagreement already exists on day one and only grows costlier. Settle purpose, authority, money and exit before the walk begins.

part2-two-are-better-than-one.reason: Argues Ecclesiastes 4 from the failure state early, but the plain answer for the reader (in a one-person business, nobody is left; inventory every single point of failure and name a backup) comes late.
part2-two-are-better-than-one.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Who is left standing when one partner falls? If every decision, password and relationship ends in you, nobody is. Ecclesiastes 4:10 argues for two from the worst day, not the best one: alone, everything stops; with another, it is a hard week. So the passage asks you to find every function that ends in one person and name who would carry it. Here is how the Word makes the case.
part2-two-are-better-than-one.example: THE TWO-WEEK TEST. Say you are suddenly unavailable for two weeks. Who logs into the bank? Who calls the lender who has actually met you? Who reaches the tradesman who only answers your number? Who knows which basement holds the main shutoff? Write each item down and put a name beside it. Every line with no name is a single point of failure.
part2-two-are-better-than-one.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Who is left standing when one partner falls? In a business where every blank ends in one man, nobody, and the Word says plainly, "woe to him that is alone when he falleth" (Ecclesiastes 4:10). The answer is a second cord: a partner, a hired manager, a documented successor, or trusted counsel. Fill the names in while you are well, and your worst week becomes a hard week instead of the end of the work.

teen.open: If you do everything yourself and you get sick, who keeps things going? Ecclesiastes 4 says nobody, unless someone is there to lift you up.
teen.close: So who is left standing? Only the people you have prepared ahead of time. Make sure someone else knows how to help.

senior.open: Ecclesiastes 4 makes its case for partnership from the day one person falls. The title asks who is left standing then, and in many one-person businesses the honest answer is no one.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. Someone is left standing only if you named them in advance. List every function that ends in you, and fill each blank with a partner, a manager, a successor, or counsel.

part3-unequally-yoked-what-a-yoke-actual.reason: Rebuilds the yoke image first; the plain answer (the mismatch Paul means is direction and allegiance, not speed; a slow partner is not an unequal yoke) arrives mid-lesson; ends on the exit test.
part3-unequally-yoked-what-a-yoke-actual.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why does a partner's direction matter more than their pace? Because a yoke binds two animals to one beam and one line. A slower partner can still plough a straight furrow with you. A partner pointed somewhere you cannot go pulls the whole implement off course, and the yoke gives neither of you a way out. Paul names that mismatch as one of direction and allegiance (2 Corinthians 6:14). Here is what a yoke actually is.
part3-unequally-yoked-what-a-yoke-actual.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why does direction matter more than pace? Because in a yoke, the other party's decisions become your obligations, and your exit needs his cooperation or a court. Speed, temperament and skill can be worked with. Direction cannot. So transact freely, but before you take a yoke, ask the question that matters: when this person moves somewhere I cannot follow, what happens to me, and how do I get out? Answer that, and you have weighed a partnership, not just a friendship.

teen.open: Why does where a partner is heading matter more than how fast they go? Because a yoke ties two together on one line, and you cannot pull in two directions.
teen.close: So direction beats pace. A slow partner can still go your way. A partner headed somewhere you cannot go will pull you off course.

senior.open: A yoke binds two animals to one implement and removes independent movement. The title asks why direction matters more than pace, and Paul's answer is that the mismatch he warns of is one of allegiance, not speed.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. Pace can be accommodated within a yoke; direction cannot. Before binding yourself, ask what happens when your partner moves where you cannot follow, and how you would get out.

part4-and-the-ships-were-broken.reason: Builds the Jehoshaphat case slowly; the answer (Yahweh broke the works because of the partner, and a sound deal gives no protection against an unsound partner) and the behavioural test both arrive late.
part4-and-the-ships-were-broken.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Did the ships sink for another reason? Yes. The venture was ordinary, lawful trade, yet the prophet names one cause: Jehoshaphat joined himself with a man who did very wickedly (2 Chronicles 20:35-37). A sound deal gives no protection against an unsound partner. So test the partner's character by what he has done, not by how the talks have felt. Here is how the account shows it.
part4-and-the-ships-were-broken.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why can a sound deal still fail? Because the soundness of the business cannot cover the unsoundness of the partner, and Jehoshaphat had the warning in a single sentence and built the ships anyway. Not every failure means a bad partner, but every yoke needs character diligence. Ask how this person acts when doing right costs him, how he treats people with no leverage, and what he did when he could have quietly taken advantage. Those answers can be found before you build.

teen.open: Can a good deal fail because of a bad partner? Yes. Jehoshaphat's ships broke because of who he joined, not because of the ships.
teen.close: So check the person, not just the plan. Watch how they treat people who cannot push back. That tells you what you need to know.

senior.open: Jehoshaphat's ships were ordinary ships on an ordinary route, yet the prophet attributes their loss to his partner. The title asks why a sound deal can fail, and the account answers plainly: the counterparty.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. A well-built deal does not protect you from an unsound partner. Test character by conduct, especially toward those who had no leverage, before you build anything together.

part5-let-there-be-no-strife-separate-th.reason: Opens on the herdsmen and power dynamics; the plain why (terms set at formation are fair because no one knows who will want out; in a dispute leverage wins) arrives in the second half.
part5-let-there-be-no-strife-separate-th.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why did Abram name the exit terms early? Because he moved while the quarrel was still among the herdsmen and before it reached the principals (Genesis 13:8-9). Terms agreed at the start are fair, since neither party yet knows who will want out or who will hold the leverage. Terms argued in a dispute go to whoever holds the power. Here is what Abram did, and how it transfers.
part5-let-there-be-no-strife-separate-th.example: CUT AND CHOOSE. Abram defines the division, and Lot picks his side. Say two partners write that into their formation documents: if they part, one sets the split of the properties, and the other chooses which share to take. The one drawing the line now has every reason to draw it fairly, because he may end up with either half.
part5-let-there-be-no-strife-separate-th.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why name the exit terms early? Because early is the only time both of you can afford to be generous, and the only time neither of you knows which side you will stand on. Abram protected the relationship, for they were brethren, by raising the separation himself and handing Lot the choice. So put a valuation method, a notice period and a buy-sell mechanism in the formation documents, before any dispute begins.

teen.open: Why talk about how to split up before you even start? Because at the beginning nobody knows who will want out, so the deal stays fair.
teen.close: So agree on the exit early, like Abram did. It keeps the friendship safe when things get hard later.

senior.open: Abram raised the separation with Lot before the dispute reached them, and he let Lot choose. The title asks why early, and the answer is that terms set at the start are made without knowing who will hold the leverage.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. Exit terms belong in the formation documents, agreed while both parties can still be generous. Abram's generosity was available because he moved early.

part6-the-contention-was-so-sharp.reason: Establishes the men's standing and the no-fault narrative first; the plain yes (each took a colleague and kept working, capacity doubled) and the standard come in the second half.
part6-the-contention-was-so-sharp.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Can both partners keep building after a sharp split? Yes. Paul and Barnabas parted over a hard disagreement, and Scripture assigns no fault. Barnabas took Mark to Cyprus, Paul took Silas, and the work went on in two places instead of one (Acts 15:39-40). Separation is not a failure of faith, but it carries a discipline. Here is what the account shows.
part6-the-contention-was-so-sharp.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Can both keep building after a sharp split? Yes, if both do what Paul and Barnabas did. Neither abandoned the work, ran down the other, cut off his resources, or spent years explaining how he was wronged. Each took a colleague and kept going, and the work doubled. So the test is not who was right, or even whether it ended badly. It is whether both of you are still building afterwards, instead of litigating the past.

teen.open: Can two people who split up still both do good work? Yes. Paul and Barnabas argued and parted, and both kept serving.
teen.close: So yes, both can keep building. The key is not to spend your time fighting over the past. Keep doing the work.

senior.open: Paul and Barnabas parted after a sharp disagreement, and the text assigns no blame. The title asks whether both can keep building, and the account answers yes.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. Both can keep building, provided neither abandons the work or campaigns against the other. The measure is not who was right, but whether both remain able to work afterwards.

part7-in-the-multitude-of-counsellors.reason: The decisive test (work out what you are short of: judgment calls for counsel; capital, hands or resilience call for a partner) only arrives in the final lines; the opening names the false binary but not the answer.
part7-in-the-multitude-of-counsellors.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Do you need a partner, or just a second opinion? It depends on what you are short of. If it is money, hands beside you, or a second cord when you fall, a partnership may be the right tool. If it is judgment, several good counsellors will give it to you with no equity, no vote and no liability (Proverbs 15:22). Here is how the Word makes room for that third option.
part7-in-the-multitude-of-counsellors.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Do you need a partner or a second opinion? Name what you are actually short of. Counsel cannot supply capital, carry the work, or lift you when you fall; for those, a careful partnership is the answer. But if what you lack is judgment, ask three or four people who have done the thing, with a narrow question, and pay them where it fits. A yoke is a very expensive way to buy an hour of someone's attention.

teen.open: Do you need a partner, or just good advice? Ask what you are missing. If it is ideas and experience, advice from a few wise people may be enough.
teen.close: So figure out what you really need. Money and help with the work may need a partner. Wisdom can come from good counsel without signing anything.

senior.open: Proverbs 15:22 commends many counsellors, and a counsellor takes no share of the venture. The title asks whether you need a partner or a second opinion, and the answer depends on what you lack.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. If you lack capital, hands, or resilience, a partnership may be right. If you lack judgment, seek several experienced counsellors, and keep your venture unyoked.

part8-the-people-had-a-mind-to-work.reason: Sets Nehemiah's situation first; the plain no (agreements are necessary, never sufficient; a perfect contract without a mind to work gives an orderly failure) comes mid-lesson; ends on self-examination.
part8-the-people-had-a-mind-to-work.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Can a contract build what the heart won't finish? No. Nehemiah 4:6 gives the reason the wall rose: the people had a mind to work. Good agreements prevent real failures, but without that disposition a perfect contract only guarantees the failure will be orderly. So choose partners by what is in them, watched over time. Here is how the account shows it.
part8-the-people-had-a-mind-to-work.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Can a contract build what the heart won't finish? No. Agreement, structure, exit terms and counsel are all necessary, and none is sufficient. Without a mind to work, the paperwork delivers a well-documented disappointment with nobody at fault. So watch for it over time: does this person show up, carry his share when no one is measuring, and want the thing done? Then ask the same of yourself, honestly, because the wall gets built by people who want it finished.

teen.open: Can a perfect agreement make people finish the work? No. Nehemiah's wall got built because the people wanted to work.
teen.close: So pick partners who show up and finish things. And make sure you are that kind of person too.

senior.open: Nehemiah 4:6 gives the cause of the built wall as the people's mind to work. The title asks whether a contract can supply that, and the answer is no.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. Sound agreements are necessary but never sufficient. Look for a mind to work by observing conduct over time, and examine your own heart with the same honesty.
